query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In multiprincipal-element alloys (MPEAs) used at high temperature in oxidizing environments, oxidation resistance and long-term material integrity are governed primarily by whether the alloy forms and retains a continuous, slow-growing external α-Al2O3 scale. This is determined by the surface chemical activity of Al exceeding a critical threshold set by temperature and oxygen partial pressure. When this threshold is exceeded, a connected Al-rich sub-surface network feeds selective oxidation to α-Al2O3; the resulting oxide grows by inward oxygen transport with low defect density, minimizing cation vacancy flux, voiding, and spallation. Alloys below this Al-activity threshold instead form mixed chromia/spinel scales that grow faster, spall more readily, and cause deeper sub-surface depletion, degrading integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase FCC Co–Ni–Cr–Fe-based MPEA with sub-threshold Al content (e.g., ~5–7 at.% Al), homogenized and solutionized to eliminate secondary phases, sulfur/phosphorus <10 ppm, equiaxed grains 30–50 µm, mirror-polished surfaces, no reactive-element additions.
generation.intervention: Increase effective Al activity while preserving single-phase FCC and similar grain size, by raising Al content by ~3–5 at.% (e.g., to ~8–12 at.% Al, compositionally constrained to stay single-phase at test temperature) without changing other base elements; optional sub-variant with a minor reactive-element addition (e.g., 0.02–0.1 at.% Y) to isolate the adhesion effect.
generation.conditions: Dry air (pO2 ≈ 0.21 atm) or controlled oxygen (10−3–1 atm O2), 1000–1150 °C, isothermal exposures of 100–200 h plus 50–100 thermal cycles (1 h at temperature, forced-air cool to <200 °C), humidity <0.1% to avoid chromia volatilization artifacts, no salts/sulfates/halides present.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous α-Al2O3 scale with low porosity and low defect density fed by a connected, surface-adjacent Al-rich zone; in the reactive-element sub-variant, Y segregation to oxide grain boundaries and the metal/oxide interface that pins the scale and suppresses voiding.
generation.mechanism: When Al activity exceeds a critical threshold for the given T and pO2, selective oxidation produces external α-Al2O3 rather than internal Al oxidation or competing chromia/spinel formation. α-Al2O3 growth proceeds predominantly by inward oxygen transport through a dense anion-conducting oxide, yielding a low parabolic mass-gain rate and minimal cation vacancy flux. This reduces Kirkendall porosity at the interface and limits sub-surface depletion. In contrast, below-threshold alloys form chromia/spinel scales that grow faster via mixed cation/anion transport, produce more voids, and spall more readily; depletion zones deepen, diminishing load-bearing cross-section and creep strength. Minor reactive-element additions further reduce scale growth and enhance adhesion by blocking fast diffusion along oxide grain boundaries and relieving interfacial stresses.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline sub-threshold alloy, the high-Al-activity alloy will: (a) transition to and maintain a continuous α-Al2O3 scale within 10–50 h at 1100 °C; (b) exhibit a lower parabolic oxidation rate constant (expected decrease on the order of a factor of ~3–10, acknowledging uncertainty in exact magnitude); (c) show shallower Al-depletion depths beneath the scale; (d) show fewer and smaller spallation events during thermal cycling, with higher retained net mass and less thickness loss; and (e) retain higher post-exposure tensile/creep strength due to reduced section loss and less sub-surface damage. The reactive-element sub-variant (if applied) will further reduce spallation frequency at comparable kp.
generation.baseline: The same base MPEA at lower Al activity (original Al content, no reactive elements), processed to the same grain size and surface finish, exposed under identical oxidizing conditions. Baseline behavior is mixed chromia/spinel external scales (and/or transient alumina that does not stabilize as α-Al2O3), higher parabolic mass-gain rates, deeper depletion zones, and more frequent spallation during thermal cycling.
generation.boundary: Expected to hold for single-phase FCC or BCC MPEAs that can sustain a connected Al supply to the surface without forming brittle intermetallic networks, at temperatures ≥900–950 °C (where α-Al2O3 can stabilize) and oxygen partial pressures ≥10−4 atm in dry environments. May not hold in high water-vapor or salt-laden atmospheres (hot corrosion, chromia volatilization), for alloys with insufficient Al mobility due to trapping in stable ordered phases, for microstructures with extreme grain refinement that disrupt Al percolation to the surface, or for refractory MPEAs prone to pesting at intermediate temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The precise Al-activity threshold for α-Al2O3 external scale formation in multicomponent matrices is composition- and temperature-dependent and not known a priori. Interactions with Cr, Ti, and other strong oxide formers can shift phase selection and kinetics. Water vapor can destabilize chromia and alter the apparent advantage of alumina. The effect size (kp reduction, spallation frequency) will depend on processing history, residual impurities (S, P), and thermal cycling profile.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two equiaxed, single-phase FCC Co–Ni–Cr–Fe–Al alloys with matched grain size and identical processing: Alloy L (low Al activity, e.g., ~6 at.% Al) and Alloy H (higher Al activity, e.g., +3–5 at.% Al while preserving single-phase at test temperature). Optional third alloy HY = Alloy H + 0.05 at.% Y for adhesion isolation. Confirm single-phase at test temperature by in-situ/high-T XRD. Expose polished coupons of each alloy to dry air at 1100 °C: (i) isothermal for 100 h and 200 h; (ii) 100 thermal cycles (1 h hot/air cool). Include inert markers (e.g., Pt) at the initial surface to identify growth direction. After exposure, characterize mass change vs time, oxide phase/continuity, growth mechanism, spallation, sub-surface depletion, and mechanical property retention.
measurements: Mass gain vs time to extract parabolic rate constants (kp)
XRD/Raman of surface oxide to identify α-Al2O3 vs chromia/spinels
Cross-sectional SEM/TEM with EDS/EELS maps for oxide continuity, porosity, and Al-depletion depth
Marker experiment outcome (marker location) to determine dominant growth direction
Acoustic emission or optical monitoring to quantify spallation events during cycling
Adhesion energy or spallation fraction via bend tests after oxidation
Post-exposure tensile or small-punch/creep tests to assess retained mechanical integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if, under the stated conditions, Alloy H does not form and maintain a continuous α-Al2O3 external scale within 100 h and does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in kp relative to Alloy L (e.g., less than 50% reduction), or if spallation incidence of Alloy H is not lower than Alloy L during thermal cycling. Observation that Alloy H persistently forms chromia/spinel as the dominant external scale under these conditions also falsifies the mechanism as stated.
